opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was one of those periods that felt kind of bleak while I was in it, and only later did I realize how much it shaped me.

London in winter is dark. The sun sets around four in the afternoon, it's gray and drizzly most days, and you spend a lot of time indoors staring at training curves. RL at that time was also notoriously finicky. You'd change a random seed and the whole result would flip. So there was this doubled sense of gloom: the weather outside, and the instability inside the experiments.

But I think it taught me a few important things. First, it made me humble about empirical results. In RL you learn very quickly that one good run means almost nothing; you need to be careful, rigorous, and honest with yourself about what's real signal and what's noise. That habit carried over into everything I did later in vision and representation learning.

Second, it changed how I think about what the "right" problem is. RL frames intelligence as an agent acting in the world, getting feedback, improving. I found that perspective really compelling, even though I eventually moved back toward vision and generative modeling. Today, when people talk about world models, embodied agents, or RL on top of foundation models, I feel those threads connecting back to what I was struggling with then.

And third, on a personal level, I learned I needed to find meaning in the process rather than the outcome. When experiments don't work for weeks, and it's dark outside by the time you've had lunch, you have to genuinely enjoy the thinking itself. Otherwise you don't last. So I look back on it with a kind of fondness now. It was a cold winter, but a formative one.

r001.rationale: The response describes the period as bleak and says he needed to enjoy the thinking process, but it does not say he suspected he did not actually enjoy RL research. It instead calls the perspective compelling and looks back with fondness.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, that winter in London was honestly one of the most confusing periods of my research life, and also one of the most formative.

I went there thinking I would just pick up another toolkit. I'd been doing vision for years, and RL felt like this neighboring field that everyone talked about but that I'd never actually touched hands-on. What I found out pretty quickly was that the culture was completely different. In vision, you set up a benchmark, you run your experiments, and the numbers tell you a story fairly fast. In RL, I'd run the same experiment with five seeds and get five different stories. The first few weeks I genuinely thought I was doing something wrong.

And the weather didn't help. It gets dark at four in the afternoon, it's grey, it rains, and you're sitting there staring at reward curves that refuse to go up. There's a particular kind of loneliness in that. You start questioning whether you understand anything at all.

But what I took away was actually really valuable. One, it taught me humility about what "it works" means. RL forced me to think much harder about variance, about evaluation, about whether a result is real or just noise. I carried that back into my vision work, and I think it made me a more careful researcher.

Two, it changed how I think about representation. In vision we often treat representation learning as the end goal. Spending time with RL people, you realize representation is only interesting if it helps an agent do something. That framing stuck with me, and honestly a lot of what I think about now, with world models and agents that act in environments, traces back to those conversations.

So if I'm honest, I didn't produce my best papers that winter. But I came out with a different set of questions, and in research, the questions you carry matter more than any single result. The London winter was the price of admission for that.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the London period as confusing, lonely, and formative, but never says Saining suspected he did not enjoy RL research.

With RL, you can spend a lot of time trying to understand what an experiment is actually telling you. Is the idea wrong, or is something in the setup preventing it from working? That uncertainty can be frustrating, but it also makes you more careful about drawing conclusions. I don’t want to overstate how much the season shaped the experience, though.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, what stands out is the uncertainty of the research process. With RL, you could spend a lot of time running experiments and still struggle to understand why something worked—or why it didn’t. That could be frustrating, especially during a dark London winter, when it was easy to feel like you were spending the whole day inside with the same problem.

But I think that was valuable, too. It pushed me to ask whether an experiment was actually helping me understand something, rather than just producing another result. Even when the immediate progress felt slow, that was a useful lesson to take away.

r001.rationale: The response describes uncertainty and frustration during RL research, but does not say Saining began to suspect he did not enjoy the research.
